One of the other two is the town where a man was kept dead a hundred years and then shown that his food had not spoiled.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The man's final sentence is a correct confession offered at the point where it changes nothing about his garden, which raises the question the parable is built around: he could have said it any morning for years. The passage also identifies his fault precisely. He never worshipped an idol; he associated his own permanence with God's, which the Quran counts under the same name.

crossReferences.why: Completes the scene, noting he had no faction to help him and that authority belongs to God.
Uses the same phrase for a town fallen in on its supports, there as a lesson about revival.
Records a confession made as the water closes in, and the answer that it comes too late.

studies.applyIt: There is a sentence you would say if you lost something you currently have. Say it now, while you still have the thing. It costs nothing today and it is the entire difference between the two men in this parable, one of whom said it walking in and one of whom said it standing in the wreckage.

studies.title: There Authority Belongs To God
studies.meaning: The second thing he boasted of fails as completely as the first. He had no body of supporters to help him and could not help himself, which answers his earlier claim about manpower directly. The ayah then makes a general statement: in a moment like that, protection belongs to God, the True. Commentators read the same word in two ways, as protective friendship or as sovereign authority, and note that the sentence works under either reading.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a city organised around clan protection. A man without backing had no legal standing, no redress and no safety, and the early believers who had been disowned knew this precisely. The parable's ending speaks to both sides of that arrangement at once: to those who relied on their faction and to those who had lost theirs.

keyTerms.note: A body of men who stand with you, used in the Quran for parties in battle. It names the practical form of protection in Arabia, which is why its absence here is a complete verdict.

From a root meaning nearness, giving both a protector who stands close and a ruler who holds power. Early readers vocalised the word two ways and the commentators accept both, since either sense fits.
From the root for a heel and for following behind. The word names what comes at the end of a sequence, so it grades the whole story rather than any single moment in it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Protection in Arabia was a formal thing, publicly declared and publicly withdrawn. A clan announced that a man was under its cover, and that announcement was what kept him alive on the road and solvent in the market. When cover was lifted, everyone knew within days. The parable's owner discovers the limit of an arrangement that ordinarily worked very well.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for protection in the second ayah was read with two different vowels by early reciters, giving either the friendship of a protector or the authority of a ruler. Both readings are preserved in the classical tradition, and commentators generally present them side by side rather than choosing, since the ayah supports each.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage does not say that human help is worthless. It says that at a certain point there is only one source of it, and it names that source with a word carrying both closeness and command. Reward and outcome are then both graded as God's, which closes the parable by moving from the man's ruined estate to a general statement about how anything ends.

crossReferences.why: Contains the boast about supporters that this ayah answers, word against word.
A man swallowed by the earth with no group to help him and no power to help himself.
States that God alone is the protecting friend, and that He gives life to the dead.

studies.applyIt: Make a short list of what you would turn to first if something serious went wrong: a person, a savings account, a professional contact. Do not cross anything off. Just look at the list and notice that you made it without effort, and that this ayah is describing the moment after every item on it has been tried.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Debris Scattered By The Wind
studies.meaning: A second parable follows immediately, and it compresses the first one into a single image. Water comes down, plants take it up and mingle with it, and then the whole growth becomes dry fragments that the wind carries off. The commentators note the speed of the sentence, which moves from rain to debris without a pause. The closing clause names God as having complete power over everything, which is what makes both the growth and the scattering His.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has just shown a wealthy man losing an estate, and this parable generalises that case so it is not read as one unlucky owner. Rain in Arabia was sudden, brief and transformative, so the audience did not need the comparison explained. They had watched a valley turn green and then turn brown inside a few weeks.

keyTerms.note: A reciprocal verb for two things becoming intertwined. The plants do not simply receive the water; they mix with it, which is why their drying is a separation as much as a death.
Vegetation broken into brittle fragments, occurring only here in the Quran. The word names the texture rather than the state, so it describes what the growth feels like in the hand once it is over.
To winnow, the verb for tossing threshed grain into the air so chaff blows away. Applying it here makes the wind a sorter, not just a destroyer, which fits a passage about what remains.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Winnowing was ordinary work. After threshing, grain was thrown up in the air on a breezy afternoon so the heavy seed fell back and the light husk blew off. Every farming household did it and every listener had watched it. The parable uses that familiar action to describe the whole of worldly life, with the sorting already built into the picture.
studies.didYouKnow: The instruction to set out a parable for them appears three times in the Quran, and two of those occurrences are in this surah, opening the story of the two gardens and opening this one. The two parables are placed thirteen ayat apart and the second is a fifth the length of the first.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The comparison is not to death but to a cycle in which growth and dispersal belong to the same process. Nothing in the image is wasted or wrong; the plants did what plants do. What is corrected is only the expectation of permanence. Naming God's complete power at the end keeps the passage from reading as a lament about time, since the sequence is described as governed rather than merely observed.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same comparison at greater length, adding the moment people think they have mastered the land.
Sets the same image inside a list of what worldly life consists of, ending in withered debris.
Follows immediately, naming what lasts once the wind has carried the rest away.

studies.applyIt: Think of something that filled your attention completely five years ago and that you have not thought about in months. Not a loss, just a thing that mattered enormously and then dispersed. Naming one is enough. The parable is not asking you to care less today; it is asking you to notice that this has already happened, repeatedly, without your permission.

studies.title: The Things That Last
studies.meaning: Two things are named and neither is condemned. Wealth and children are called the ornament of this life, which grants that their attraction is real and located exactly where the surah placed it earlier. Set against them is a phrase left deliberately open: the lasting good things. The commentators offer a range for what it covers, from remembrance and prayer to any righteous act, and most decline to narrow it. The comparison is made twice, in reward and in hope.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The ayah follows the parable of the man with two gardens who told his companion he had more wealth and a stronger following, and whose gardens were destroyed overnight. It also follows the image of the world as vegetation that rain raises and wind scatters. The commentators report no specific occasion. Placing the ayah there makes it the conclusion of a story rather than a general maxim.

keyTerms.note: An active participle of remaining, in the feminine plural, with no noun attached. The absence is what makes the phrase famous: it names a category and leaves the reader to fill it.
From a root meaning to come back. The reward is described as something returning to the one who sent it out, which is a different picture from a prize handed over at the end.
The word for what a person leans forward towards. Saying the lasting things are better as hope means they are the better thing to want, which is a claim about the present rather than the future.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth and sons were the two measures of a man in that society, and they were connected. Sons meant hands for the herd, riders in a feud, and someone to keep your name. A rich man with no sons was pitied; a poor man with many was still counted. Naming exactly those two as ornament was naming the whole scoring system the audience used on each other.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about the lasting good things appears twice in the Quran, here and in another Meccan surah, both times in the same phrase and both times in a comparison. Reports from the companions attach it to particular phrases of remembrance, while many commentators keep it wide. Both readings have circulated side by side since the earliest period.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah does not ask anyone to stop valuing wealth or children. It ranks them, which is a different operation, and it ranks them by duration rather than by worth. That leaves ordinary attachments intact while removing their claim to be ultimate. The second comparison is the sharper one. Saying the lasting things are better as hope reaches into what a person spends the day wanting, which is harder to adjust than what they spend it doing.

crossReferences.why: The other occurrence of the same phrase, closing on return rather than on hope.
The parable this ayah concludes, about a man whose two gardens made him certain.
Lists the same attractions in more detail and calls them the enjoyment of this life.

studies.applyIt: Ask yourself what you hoped for when you woke up this morning. Not what you believe you should hope for: the actual first thought. Write it down in five words. Then leave the note somewhere you will see it in a week. This ayah compares two hopes rather than two possessions, and the comparison only works if you know what yours is.

studies.title: The Earth Laid Bare
studies.meaning: Three things happen in one sentence. The mountains are set moving, the earth appears stripped and level, and everyone is gathered with no one left out. The commentators read the middle clause as the removal of everything that stood on the surface, so the ground is shown without its features. The final clause is the one that carries the weight: not a single person is passed over, which turns a cosmic scene into a personal one.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Descriptions of the last day in the early revelations are short, physical and delivered without argument, addressed to people who found the idea of universal gathering implausible. This ayah arrives just after two parables about things that looked permanent, so the dissolution of mountains reads as the same lesson at maximum scale.

keyTerms.note: The verb for making something travel, used of caravans and of clouds. Applied to mountains it does not say they are destroyed, only that the least movable thing in the landscape is made to go somewhere.
Something that has come out into the open with nothing in front of it. Occurring only here in this form, it presents the earth as exposed rather than damaged, a surface with no cover left.
A verb for leaving something out, related to the word for treachery, since to abandon a person is to break faith. Used in the negative it says the gathering has no omissions and no exceptions.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mountains were the fixed reference of Arabian life. Travellers navigated by peaks, tribal territories were described by them, and a mountain on the horizon was how you knew where you were. Nothing in the visible world was more permanent. A description of them being made to move would have registered as the removal of the last thing anyone could steer by.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb saying that no one will be left out appears only once in the Quran, and its root is the same one behind the Arabic word for treachery, the breaking of a trust. The choice quietly frames being overlooked at the gathering as a betrayal that will not occur.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage answers a specific anxiety about universal judgement, which is that individuals get lost in a large number. Its final clause denies exactly that. It also completes a movement running through the surah, where things assumed to be stable are shown to be held in place rather than fixed by nature: sleepers, gardens, harvests and now mountains.

crossReferences.why: Describes the mountains scattered as dust and the earth left as a level plain with no crookedness.
Lists the folding of the sun and the moving of the mountains among the signs of that day.
The parable just before, where the same lesson about impermanence is drawn from a season of rain.

studies.applyIt: Look at the largest fixed thing you can see from where you are, a building, a hill, a road. Hold it for a moment as something that has a duration rather than as background. This ayah is not asking for dread. It is asking you to move one item from the category of permanent to the category of long, which is a change you can actually make.

studies.title: If The Ocean Were Ink
studies.meaning: The surah ends by placing three very different things side by side. First a garden described as hospitality, a word for what a host sets out on arrival, with no wish to be moved from it. Then an image of scale: the sea would run dry before the words of the Lord did, and another sea after it. Then a final instruction that reduces everything to two conditions, righteous work and worship with nothing else added underneath it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing a surah that answered questions put by opponents to test the message. The classical sources report a specific occasion for the last ayah in some accounts, concerning a man who prayed and also wanted to be seen praying, though the reports differ and several commentators leave it general. The ayah about the sea is reported in connection with a question about how much knowledge had been given.

keyTerms.note: The word for what a host lays out for a guest on arrival, before the real hosting begins. Calling the garden that suggests it is the reception rather than the whole of what is coming.
From a root meaning to extend or supply, the same root as the word for reinforcement used two clauses later. The image and its answer are built from one root, which the translation cannot show.
The word for a person considered as flesh and skin, rather than the word that emphasises the human as a species or a soul. It is the plainest available term, which is the point of the sentence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Ink was made from soot and gum and kept in small quantities, and writing was a specialist trade. A scribe measured his supply carefully, and running out mid-document was a real interruption. Setting the sea against an inkwell was not a poetic flourish to people who had watched one being refilled. The comparison worked because everyone knew how little ink a person actually had.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah opens with praise for a Book with no crookedness and closes by saying the words of the Lord would outlast the sea as ink. Its first and last movements are both about the extent of revelation. The word used for the garden here appears only twice in the Quran, and this is one of the two places.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The last ayah does two things at once. It denies the messenger any status beyond being human and receiving revelation, which removes him as an object of devotion in the same breath as it establishes his role. And it states the whole requirement in one sentence: do good work, and put nothing beside God in the worship of God. Everything the surah has narrated, the cave, the gardens, the journey, resolves into that.

crossReferences.why: Multiplies the same image: all the trees as pens and seven seas as ink.
The other place the same word for the garden appears, promised to the heirs.
Another place the messenger is told to say he is only a human being.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you did this week for a good reason and ask what the second reason was. There usually is one, and it is usually about how it looked. Do not scold yourself. Just find the next occasion to do the same thing where nobody will know, and see whether you still want to. That is the test this ayah sets.
